rooms.title: Processes & Threads
rooms.summary: What a process is, its states, fork(), and how threads share a process's memory.
rooms.boss_flavor: Cut off one head and fork() grows two more.

questions.prompt: What is a process?
options: A file the OS has opened
questions.explanation: A process is a program in execution, with its own address space, program counter, registers and PCB.

questions.prompt: Which of these do threads of the same process share?
questions.explanation: Threads share code, heap, global data and open files; each thread keeps its own stack, registers and program counter.

questions.prompt: A running process requests to read from disk. Which state transition happens?
questions.explanation: Requesting I/O moves a process from Running to Waiting until the I/O completes.

questions.prompt: Why is switching between threads of the same process cheaper than switching between processes?
options: The address space and page tables don't change
Threads have no registers to save
The OS skips the scheduler for threads
questions.explanation: Threads share the process's address space, so the page tables don't need to change on a switch.

questions.prompt: A program runs fork(); fork(); fork(); in sequence. How many processes exist in total, including the original?
questions.explanation: Each fork doubles the processes running it, so three sequential forks give 2^3 = 8 processes.

questions.prompt: A child process has exited, but it still appears in the process table. What is the most likely reason?
options: It is an orphan waiting for init
Its parent hasn't called wait() yet — it's a zombie
It is stuck in the Waiting state for I/O
The scheduler hasn't picked it yet
questions.explanation: A zombie has terminated but its parent hasn't called wait() to collect its exit status.

rooms.title: CPU Scheduling
rooms.summary: How the scheduler picks the next process: FCFS, SJF, priority and Round Robin.
rooms.boss_flavor: It gives everyone a turn. Including its fists.

questions.prompt: Which scheduling algorithm suffers from the convoy effect?
questions.explanation: In FCFS, short jobs queue behind one long job — the convoy effect.

questions.prompt: What does Round Robin give each process before moving it to the back of the queue?
questions.explanation: Round Robin runs each process for a fixed time quantum, then preempts it.

questions.prompt: Shortest Job First is provably optimal for minimising what?
questions.explanation: SJF minimises average waiting time, though it needs burst lengths in advance.

questions.prompt: Low-priority processes never get the CPU under priority scheduling. What fixes this?
questions.explanation: Aging gradually raises the priority of waiting processes, preventing starvation.

questions.prompt: P1=6, P2=2, P3=4 (burst times) all arrive at time 0. What is the average waiting time under SJF?
questions.explanation: SJF runs P2, P3, P1 with waits 0, 2 and 6 → (0+2+6)/3 = 2.67.

questions.prompt: What happens to Round Robin as the time quantum becomes very large?
questions.explanation: If the quantum exceeds every burst, each process runs to completion in arrival order — FCFS.

rooms.title: Process Synchronization
rooms.summary: Race conditions, critical sections, mutexes, spinlocks and semaphores.
rooms.boss_flavor: Only one of you may fight it at a time.

questions.prompt: What is a critical section?
options: Code that runs with the highest priority
Code accessing shared resources that only one process may run at a time
The part of the kernel that handles interrupts
A section of memory reserved for the OS
questions.explanation: A critical section accesses shared resources and must not be executed by more than one process at once.

questions.prompt: What does a mutex lock guarantee?
questions.explanation: A mutex provides mutual exclusion: acquire before the critical section, release after.

questions.prompt: Which three properties must a correct critical-section solution provide?
questions.explanation: A correct solution provides mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting.

questions.prompt: A counting semaphore is initialised to 3. What does that allow?
options: Up to 3 processes using the resource at once
A 3 ms time limit in the critical section
questions.explanation: A counting semaphore initialised to N lets up to N processes use the resource concurrently.

questions.prompt: counter = 5. Two threads each run counter++ once with no lock. Which final values are possible?
questions.explanation: counter++ is read-modify-write. If both read 5 before either writes, one update is lost and the result is 6; otherwise it's 7.

questions.prompt: When is a busy-waiting spinlock a reasonable choice?
options: On a single-core CPU with long critical sections
On a multiprocessor when the lock is held very briefly
Whenever a process performs disk I/O inside the lock
questions.explanation: On multiprocessors with very short critical sections, spinning is cheaper than a context switch.

rooms.title: Deadlocks
rooms.summary: The four Coffman conditions and how to prevent, avoid or detect deadlock.
rooms.boss_flavor: Break one chain and he falls. Which one?

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the four Coffman conditions for deadlock?
questions.explanation: The condition is NO preemption. The four are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait.

questions.prompt: What is a deadlock?
options: A set of processes each waiting for a resource held by another in the set
A process that has finished but wasn't reaped
Two processes running the same program
questions.explanation: In a deadlock, every process in the set waits on a resource held by another process in the set.

questions.prompt: The Banker's algorithm is used for deadlock…
questions.explanation: The Banker's algorithm avoids deadlock by granting requests only if the system stays in a safe state.

questions.prompt: Requiring every process to acquire resources in one fixed global order breaks which condition?
questions.explanation: A total ordering on resource acquisition makes a cycle of waits impossible, preventing circular wait.

questions.prompt: 3 processes each need at most 2 instances of a resource, and there are 5 instances in total. Can they deadlock?
options: Yes, if each holds one instance
No — even if each holds one, spare instances let one finish
questions.explanation: n(m−1)+1 = 3×1+1 = 4 ≤ 5, so a spare instance always lets some process finish.

questions.prompt: A resource-allocation graph has a cycle, and each resource has several instances. What can you conclude?
options: A deadlock is possible but not certain
questions.explanation: With multiple instances, a cycle means deadlock is possible but not guaranteed. With single instances it would be certain.

rooms.title: Memory Management & Paging
rooms.summary: Pages, frames, page tables, the TLB and effective access time.
rooms.boss_flavor: It remembers where everything lives. Mostly.

questions.prompt: Which problem does paging eliminate?
questions.explanation: Fixed-size frames eliminate external fragmentation, though a little internal fragmentation remains.

questions.prompt: What does a page table map?
questions.explanation: The page table translates page numbers into physical frame numbers.

questions.prompt: With 4 KB pages, how many bits of a logical address are the page offset?
questions.explanation: 4 KB = 2^12 bytes, so the offset needs 12 bits.

questions.prompt: What is the TLB?
options: A backup copy of the disk
A fast cache of page-table entries
questions.explanation: The Translation Lookaside Buffer caches recent page-table entries to speed up translation.

questions.prompt: 32-bit logical addresses, 4 KB pages and 4-byte page-table entries: how big is a single-level page table?
TLB hit ratio 80%, memory access 100 ns, TLB lookup time negligible. What is the effective access time?
questions.explanation: EAT = 0.8 × 100 + 0.2 × 200 = 120 ns — a miss needs one extra memory access for the page table.

rooms.title: Virtual Memory & Page Replacement
rooms.summary: Demand paging, page faults, FIFO/LRU/Optimal replacement, Belady's anomaly and thrashing.
rooms.boss_flavor: It spends more time swapping than swinging.

questions.prompt: When does a page fault occur?
options: When a page is written to
When a referenced page is not in main memory
When two processes share a page
questions.explanation: A page fault happens when the referenced page isn't in RAM and must be loaded from disk.

questions.prompt: Under demand paging, when is a page loaded into memory?
options: Only when it is first referenced
questions.explanation: Demand paging loads a page only when it is first needed.

questions.prompt: Which replacement policy can suffer from Belady's anomaly?
questions.explanation: With FIFO, adding frames can increase page faults — Belady's anomaly. LRU and Optimal are immune.

questions.prompt: What is thrashing?
options: Spending more time paging than executing
Two threads racing for a lock
A process being starved by the scheduler
questions.explanation: Thrashing happens when processes lack frames for their working sets and the system mostly pages.

questions.prompt: Reference string 7, 0, 1, 2, 0, 3, 0, 4 with 3 frames and FIFO. How many page faults?
questions.explanation: Faults on 7, 0, 1, 2, 3, 0 and 4 — only the first reuse of 0 hits, so 7 faults.

questions.prompt: Same string 7, 0, 1, 2, 0, 3, 0, 4 with 3 frames, but LRU. How many page faults?
questions.explanation: LRU evicts 7, then 1, then 2; both reuses of 0 hit, so 6 faults.
